q: When food is scarce on Wolf Island in the Galápagos, some ground finches supplement their diet with what from living seabirds?
d: They peck near feather bases and lap the blood that emerges.
s: Natural History Museum · Blood-loving Galápagos birds
evidence: Museum explains finches pecking Nazca boobies until bleeding and lapping blood.

q: Tracking devices revealed that some common swifts spent their entire ten-month nonbreeding period doing what?
d: Some tracked birds showed no landing at all; others made occasional stops.
s: Hedenström and colleagues · Common swift aerial life
evidence: Primary abstract reports over99% airborne time and no settling in some individuals.

q: Unlike most fishes, mudskippers blink. What moves during their unusual blink?
a: The eye retracts into its socket
d: A skin cup rises around the withdrawing eye, helping wet, clean and protect it on land.
choices: A lower eyelid rises over the eye
The eye retracts into its socket
A side membrane sweeps across the eye
s: Aiello and colleagues · Origin of blinking
evidence: Primary study documents eye retraction with passive dermal-cup movement.

q: In some deep-sea anglerfish species, what becomes of a tiny male after he attaches to a female?
d: Their tissues unite and establish shared blood circulation.
choices: He detaches after a brief mating
He lives in her nest without attaching
He releases sperm while swimming nearby
s: University of Washington · Anglerfish immune systems
evidence: Study account describes permanent attachment, tissue fusion and common circulation in specified species.

q: How can a beaver gnaw underwater without opening the inside of its mouth to the water?
a: Seal its lips behind its incisors
d: The cutting teeth remain outside the closed lips.
choices: Close its lips around each individual tooth
Hold water in expandable cheek pouches
Seal its lips behind its incisors
Press its tongue over the nostrils
s: New York City Wildlife · Beavers
evidence: City wildlife account states lips close behind teeth during underwater gnawing.

q: How does a manatee replace grinding teeth worn down by gritty plant food?
a: New molars advance from the back
d: Teeth move forward along the jaw like a conveyor belt, with worn front teeth eventually falling out.
choices: New molars advance from the back
All molars are shed together each year
Old molars regrow enamel from their tips
New teeth rise directly under each old tooth
s: Smithsonian Ocean · Meet the sirenians
evidence: Account explains lifelong marching molars emerging behind and progressing forward.

q: What practical protection does the hippo’s reddish skin secretion provide?
d: The substance also helps keep its skin moist; it is neither ordinary sweat nor blood.
s: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance · Hippo
evidence: Zoo describes red secretion protecting skin from sunburn and dehydration.

q: How does a hippo usually propel itself through deeper water?
d: It walks or bounds along the riverbed instead of swimming with sustained paddling.
choices: Paddle with its front feet only
Undulate its whole body like an eel
s: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance · Hippo
evidence: Zoo describes bottom walking and pushing off because hippos are too dense to float.

q: How can a sleeping hippo replenish its air while resting underwater?
d: An automatic reflex lets it rise, inhale and sink back down.
choices: Sleep only with the nostrils exposed
s: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance · Hippo
evidence: Zoo explicitly describes reflexive surfacing and breathing during sleep.

q: Many female hornbills raise their chicks inside a tree cavity with what unusual entrance arrangement?
a: A sealed wall with a narrow feeding slit
d: The male delivers food through the opening while the female remains enclosed.
choices: A sealed wall with a narrow feeding slit
A leaf curtain moved aside for each meal
An open entrance guarded by both adults
s: Los Angeles Zoo · Hornbills
evidence: Zoo describes female and male sealing cavity entrance with mud, droppings and food remains.

q: What makes the long fangs of the dragonfish Aristostomias scintillans especially hard for prey to detect?
d: Their microscopic structure greatly reduces light scattering.
s: UC San Diego · Transparent dragonfish teeth
evidence: Researchers report nanostructured transparent teeth with reduced scattering and absent dentin tubules.

q: Some deep-sea dragonfish illuminate prey with what color that most neighboring fish cannot see?
d: They can produce and detect long-wavelength light in an otherwise dark habitat.
s: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution · Stoplight loosejaw
evidence: WHOI describes red light organs and red vision in Malacosteus, invisible to most other fish.

q: Playing recordings of a kea’s distinctive warbling call caused nearby parrots to do more of what?
d: Both juveniles and adults increased playful behavior during the experiment.
s: Schwing and colleagues · Positive emotional contagion
evidence: Primary abstract reports increased play after acoustic playback of play calls.

q: When a task required piercing a barrier and then extracting a nut, what did some Goffin’s cockatoos bring to the work site?
d: They could transport a set suited to a task, rather than fetch every tool only after needing it.
choices: An unopened nut as a substitute
s: Osuna-Mascaró and colleagues · Flexible tool-set transport
evidence: Primary paper reports flexible use and transport of two-tool sets.

q: In a controlled study, juvenile American alligators stayed underwater longer after swallowing what?
d: The results fit the idea that added ballast allows more air to be carried in the lungs.
s: Uriona and colleagues · Lithophagy and dives
evidence: Granite ingestion increased average and maximum voluntary dive durations; mechanism presented as supported hypothesis.

q: What useful information does a honeybee’s waggle dance convey to other foragers?
d: The movement encodes a route from the hive to a rewarding location.
choices: Size and temperature of the brood
Age and fertility of the queen
Identity and number of nearby predators
s: University of Sussex · Decoding waggle dances
evidence: Laboratory research summary identifies direction and distance of profitable flower patches.

q: When threatened by a partly submerged conductor, an electric eel can strengthen its shock by doing what?
a: Rising out of the water against it
d: The eel presses its chin against the target and delivers pulses through direct contact.
choices: Rising out of the water against it
Striking it repeatedly with the tail
s: Vanderbilt University · Leaping electric eels
evidence: Catania measured increasing electrical effect during upward contact with conducting targets.

q: An archerfish’s water shot packs extra force at its target because what happens during flight?
a: The rear of the jet catches its front
d: Timing adjustments concentrate the water just before impact.
choices: The stream breaks into separated droplets
The stream rotates around its axis
The rear of the jet catches its front
The stream spreads into a broad fan
s: Journal of Experimental Biology · Archerfish shooting
evidence: Primary paper describes later water catching the front at a timing adjusted to target distance.

q: Why can a sabretooth blenny’s resemblance to a cleaner wrasse be bad news for larger fish?
a: It bites flesh instead of cleaning
d: The mimic’s appearance and movements let it approach fish expecting parasite removal.
choices: It attacks the real cleaner fish
It steals food from their mouths
It chases them from feeding territory
It bites flesh instead of cleaning
s: University of Hawai‘i · Cleaners and mimics
evidence: Account describes blenny mimicry of cleaner wrasse and bites to client tissue.

q: Researchers photographed an albatross doing what helpful service for an ocean sunfish?
d: The fish appeared to present themselves sideways while the birds picked attached parasites.
choices: Turning it upright after a dive
Pulling seaweed out of its mouth
s: Abe and colleagues · Sunfish and albatross cleaning
evidence: Primary observation photographed a Laysan albatross taking and eating a Pennella parasite from a sunfish.

q: A jewel wasp delivers a precisely aimed sting to which part of a cockroach to suppress its urge to escape?
d: The roach can still move, but its spontaneous escape behavior is greatly reduced.
s: Gal and colleagues · Jewel wasp stinger senses
evidence: Primary experiments support mechanical sensing of brain tissue and targeted venom delivery.

q: In a mirror experiment, what did marked cleaner wrasses do after seeing a brown spot on their own throats?
a: Scrape their throats on the substrate
d: The observed response depended on the mirror and a parasite-like mark. What it demonstrates about self-awareness remains debated.
choices: Scrape their throats on the substrate
Display their fins at the reflection
Try to feed the reflected fish
Peck at the mirror’s brown spot
s: Kohda and colleagues · Cleaner-fish mirror experiments
evidence: Study reports throat scraping with brown marks and mirrors; controls without mirrors or differently colored marks did not show the same response.

q: After developing inside a cricket or another insect, where does an adult horsehair worm usually need to emerge to reproduce?
d: The long, thin parasite’s adult reproductive stage is aquatic.
s: University of Florida IFAS · Horsehair worms
evidence: Extension account describes parasitic immature stages and free-living aquatic adults; avoids overstating host mind-control.

q: The parasite Leucochloridium creates conspicuous pulsating swellings in which parts of an infected snail?
d: Colorful broodsacs occupy the tentacles. Their resemblance to caterpillars may attract the birds needed for the parasite’s life cycle.
s: Nakao and colleagues · Leucochloridium in Japan
evidence: Primary abstract describes pulsating colorful broodsacs within snail eyestalks; caterpillar mimicry is qualified as apparent.

q: A stoplight loosejaw’s red-light vision is aided by a derivative of which familiar plant pigment?
d: The unusual visual sensitizer reaches the fish through its food chain.
s: Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution · Stoplight loosejaw
evidence: WHOI links red perception to chlorophyll-related pigments acquired through copepod prey.
